To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
teachers’ beliefs about ICT and their use of ICT are related, and this relationship can be described in terms of a typology.
teachers’ beliefs about technology and their practices with it are interrelated and can be categorized in terms of the aims they have for their use.
teachers who believe technology is a tool to support learning and teaching are likely to use it in the classroom in a variety of ways.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a model of teacher beliefs and practice in relation to the use of ICT, and the implications for teacher professional development.
understanding teachers’ beliefs and practice with ICT and the relationship between these two aspects of their work.
understanding how teachers’ beliefs and practice interact in the classroom and how these interactions are related to the use of ICT in education.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
teachers’ beliefs and practice with ICT can be explained by their value for technology.

the study has provided a better understanding of the complexity of teachers’ response to the implementation of ICT in schools and that it has contributed to the literature in this area by adding to the body of knowledge about teachers’ response to ICT implementation.
there is no ‘one-size-fits-all’ approach to the use of ICT in education.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
a teacher’s beliefs and practices with respect to the use of ICT in the classroom is an outcome of a complex interaction of factors, including personal, contextual, and technological factors.
teachers who are not using technology in the classroom are not necessarily resistant to its introduction, but rather are using technology for a different purpose.
teachers’ beliefs and practice with technology are complex and varied, and that a typology can provide a framework for understanding the range of responses to ICT.
The main takeaway from our work is that

teachers’ use of educational technology in the classroom is influenced by their beliefs and practices and that these are in turn affected by the wider context of the school and the educational system.
teachers’ beliefs and practice are not static, and can be changed.

teachers’ beliefs and values are crucial in shaping the way they use ICT in the classroom and that a better understanding of these beliefs and values is essential for effective implementation of educational technology in schools.
